steps.label: KP01 Training is looking for the lowest valley
Mountain, slope, hiker · 1/7
steps.speakerNotes: Imagine being blindfolded on a mountain and having to reach the lowest valley. Training a network is exactly that.

steps.label: Mountain, slope, hiker · 1/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The mountain is the loss of every set of parameters.

steps.label: Mountain, slope, hiker · 1/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The slope is the direction the loss changes at this point, the gradient.

steps.label: Mountain, slope, hiker · 1/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The hiker is the optimizer.

steps.label: Mountain, slope, hiker · 1/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: You cannot see the whole mountain; you only feel which direction is steepest right now.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7
steps.speakerNotes: Machine learning splits training into three roles.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The hypothesis class decides which functions the model can draw, the shape the mountain may have.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The loss turns the gap between prediction and answer into a score, one for every set of parameters.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The optimizer reads the score and decides where to adjust the parameters next.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: The goal in one line: among all parameters, find the one with the smallest loss.

steps.label: Three roles · 2/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: This line says what to find, not how. A loss can say one set is better than another, but not which way to step next.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7
steps.speakerNotes: Now let us see what the optimizer does at each step.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Step one: predict with the current parameters and data.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Step two: compare with the answers and compute the loss.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Step three: take the gradient of the loss at this point, the direction of fastest increase.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Step four: choose the next parameters.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Then return to step one and repeat until stopping. When to stop is the topic of KP03.

steps.label: Four actions per step · 3/7 (6)
steps.speakerNotes: The negative gradient is the downhill direction.

steps.label: One step · 4/7
steps.speakerNotes: Use a two-parameter bowl to see the four steps. The start is 10, 2 with loss 100 and gradient 10, 50, almost along y because the bowl is much steeper there.

steps.label: One step · 4/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A step with learning rate 0.06 lands at 9.4, minus 1.0.

steps.label: One step · 4/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The new loss is 56.68, below 100: a real step downhill.

steps.label: One step · 4/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The negative gradient points almost along y because the bowl is much steeper there.

steps.label: Newton's method · 5/7
steps.speakerNotes: With gradients only the path zigzags: y is multiplied by minus 0.5 each step, shrinking with alternating signs, while x is multiplied by only 0.94, so sideways progress is slow. The loss is 14.5 at step 10 and still 1.2 at step 30.

steps.label: Newton's method · 5/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: If we also use curvature, the Hessian is diag 1, 25. Newton rescales the gradient by its inverse and lands at the origin in one step.

steps.label: Newton's method · 5/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Because the bowl is exactly quadratic, Newton is exact and the loss is 0 after the first step.

steps.label: Newton's method · 5/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: quadratic: Newton is exact, loss 0 at step 1 the gradient knows only the steepest direction; curvature says how curved the bowl is

steps.label: The curvature bill · 6/7
steps.speakerNotes: Curvature is so useful; why does deep learning not use it? Because the cost grows quickly with the number of parameters d.

steps.label: The curvature bill · 6/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal 100: gradient 400 bytes, Hessian 40 KB, inversion a million operations, 0.1 microseconds.

steps.label: The curvature bill · 6/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal ten thousand: Hessian 400 MB, inversion 10 to the 12 operations, 0.1 second.

steps.label: The curvature bill · 6/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal a million, small for today's networks: Hessian 4 TB, inversion about 27.8 hours, and that is only one step.

steps.label: The curvature bill · 6/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: The times assume a hypothetical hardware speed, so they are only order-of-magnitude estimates.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “the loss tells the optimizer which way to go”. no: the loss only scores parameters

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “the gradient points at the lowest point”. not necessarily: it is only the steepest uphill direction right now

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “second-order methods are always better”. strong on small problems, unaffordable at $d=10^6$

steps.label: Myths and next question · 7/7 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: So deep learning picks first-order methods: each step needs one gradient, which backpropagation (KP06) computes cheaply. But with only a direction, how far should one step go?
